1) constant capital requirements are capable of reducing risk below the unregulated level, and even achieve the socially efficient level of zero bankruptcy cost, but this might happen only for very high levels (e.g. 40%); 2) as the dynamic of bank risk depends on these capital requirements, and they in their turn depend upon the bank initial equity, knowing the latter is crucial for the regulator to know the effectiveness of capital requirements; and 3) additional market instruments and effective market

capital requirements are indeed capable of curbing bank risk, and that the dynamic of risk taking depends upon initial conditions, and that this is an essential piece of information for the regulator.
capital regulation is indeed a powerful tool for curbing bank risk, but it can also be very costly in terms of financial intermediation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the intertemporal effect of the capital regulation on the risk taking decisions of banks, and with how the effectiveness of this regulation depends on the initial equity of banks.
the dynamic properties of capital regulation, and the intertemporal nature of the risk taking decisions of banks.
the intertemporal aspects of capital regulation, which are not considered in the Basel II proposals, and we find that they are crucial in determining the effectiveness of the regulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

capital regulation, as proposed in Basel II, is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for reducing risk taking below unregulated levels, and for achieving socially efficient levels of bank risk taking.
the Blum model is indeed capable of explaining the observed risk taking behavior of banks, and of explaining the observed evolution in capital requirements.
Basel II and Basel I, as they stand today, are not necessarily contradictory, and that the latter could be useful for the purpose of reducing risk taking, if the former are not yet in place.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
capital regulation is indeed a very useful instrument for the regulator, as long as it is properly designed and enforced.
the Blum’s model is a useful tool for studying the effects of capital regulation on bank risk taking, and that the results are sensitive to the dynamic of risk and to the initial capital of the bank.
Basel I, as it stands, can be a good tool for the regulator to control bank risk taking, provided it is implemented correctly, and that Basel II can help the regulator on this task.
The main takeaway from our work is that
capital regulation is a very powerful tool for curbing bank risk, and that its effects are not only immediate but also intertemporal.
, while Basel II is certainly a step in the right direction, the current regulatory framework still falls short of providing a comprehensive solution to the problem of risk taking by banks.
the Basel I capital regulation, which was the first step in a long process of regulatory reform, is not a bad one, but rather a necessary first step in the right direction.
